newsitem.title: KENYA: Mombasa violence latest blow to Kenya's image.
newsitem.headline: Mombasa violence latest blow to Kenya's image.

text.p: A mysterious eruption of killings on Kenya's tourist coast is the latest blow to a troubled country beset by bad politics.
Kenya is repeatedly making news for all the wrong reasons -- political violence, unpunished corruption, a battered currency and now mayhem on the normally sleepy coast near Mombasa.

"We have had two months of stark and shocking headlines around the world. Anything which threatens the tourist industry is obviously going to be bad news for Kenya's foreign exchange earnings," a senior Western diplomat in Nairobi commented.
The only positive blip -- three golds for Kenya's renowned runners at the world athletics championships in Athens -- was quickly forgotten.
The stormy backdrop for Kenya's woes is the election that President Daniel arap Moi must call by the end of the year.
After 19 years in the presidency -- he was number two for the preceding 11 years -- the 73-year-old Moi wants another and legally final five-year term.
Moi won with less than 40 percent of the votes in 1992 when, against his will, Kenya staged its first multi-party polls.
In the absence of reliable opinion polls, pundits can only speculate on whether Moi and his ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) are any more popular today.
What is undeniable is that the East African country of nearly 30 million people is in poor political health and the fallout threatens to derail economic reforms.

The shilling hit a new low against the dollar on Monday. It has dropped nearly 20 percent since the International Monetary Fund toughened its stand on official corruption and shelved a $205 million loan.
The World Bank partially followed suit and appeals by the central bank and finance ministry have failed to stop many foreign investors from withdrawing their money.
More than a dozen people, including policemen, have died in political violence since early July.
Parts of the divided opposition are threatening civil disturbance unless political reforms are agreed before the presidential and parliamentary elections whose date Moi has not announced.
Kenyan newspapers are reporting on the growth of private political militias.
Nairobi's mayor, Dick Waweru, was beaten last week by his own council's security guards when they broke up a gathering of unemployed street hawkers, killing one.
But Kenyans were stunned when the malaise spread suddenly to the Indian Ocean coast, usually portrayed as a friendly haven where European tourists flock by the hundreds of thousands.

More than 30 people, including seven police officers, have been shot or chopped to death since August 13. Despite a vast security operation, police and the government have failed to explain the violence by organised groups of armed men.
Some of the victims were apparently targets because they were settlers from outside the coastal region.

So far no tourist has been killed or hurt and there are no significant cancellations. But some tourists have transferred to hotels further from trouble spots. Others are moving in convoys with police escorts, Auni Kanji, managing director of tour company Abercrombie and Kent, told Reuters.
"The tourists are calm, but if any of them were to get injured then it would be a disaster," Kanji said.
Moi's suggestion that opposition supporters were to blame in Mombasa seemed designed to advance his long-held view that multi-party politics is wrong for Africa because it deepens tribal enmities.
But in opposition ranks, KANU was accused of stirring up hatred in Mombasa with the elections and reform calls in mind.
"I think it's been orchestrated to look like an ethnic thing but this was well-planned," said a Nairobi printer.
"This is basically the regime saying: 'How can we have political reforms with all this violence?'"
Western diplomats were mulling the evidence.
"There are so many tensions on the coast between local people and newcomers, with land-grabbers, you name it," said one diplomat.
"But someone has decided to play with that tinderbox."
